The gap is isolation hygiene: cleanup is a bare 'delete process.env.PROOFSPEC_TMUX_SOCKET' at the tail of the test body (line 84), not an afterEach/try-finally. If the preceding expect() in the loop throws, that delete never runs and PROOFSPEC_TMUX_SOCKET leaks into every test that runs afterward in this process -- silently redirecting their tmux commands to 'proofspec-test-run-42' instead of the default. This codebase already has the correct convention for exactly this class of env var (judge-cli.test.ts uses afterEach to delete PROOFSPEC_JUDGE_BIN/PROOFSPEC_JUDGE_TIMEOUT_MS unconditionally), which session.test.ts does not follow here. Given this requirement exists specifically because ambient/global tmux state leaked and caused real damage, a test whose own cleanup of global env state isn't guaranteed is a real gap, not a nitpick.

note: The THEN claims the outcome reads unresolved once the CONFIGURED timeout elapses. But the proof (lines 85-88) only asserts elapsed time < 5000ms while PROOFSPEC_JUDGE_TIMEOUT_MS is set to 300ms -- a 16x slack. A mutation to src/cli/judge.ts:40, replacing 'const timeoutMs = judgeTimeoutMs(process.env.PROOFSPEC_JUDGE_TIMEOUT_MS)' with a hardcoded e.g. 'const timeoutMs = 2000', ignoring the env var entirely, still passes this test: the sleep-100 stand-in is still killed under 5000ms and the verdict is still {kind:'unresolved'}. So the test proves *some* timeout under 5s bounds the wait, not that the configured value is what is honored -- the 'configured' half of the THEN claim is unproven.

Only the sibling requirement's touched-inventory test catches it; this scenario's own lines do not. The harness already records the script's whole global reach (touched), so asserting here that the script touches no clock global would close it — the file's own comment elsewhere names the principle: a shape, not a list of spellings a mutant could walk around.

note: The requirement's atomicity claim (the wx-flag atomic-write idiom collapsing the check-then-create race window to one atomic filesystem call) is untested. This scenario's proof (queue.test.ts lines 65-76) only calls enqueue twice sequentially, awaiting each in turn -- never races two enqueue calls with Promise.all on the same TASK name. Swapping the wx-flag write for a non-atomic check-then-create would violate 'refuses rather than overwrite' under a real race while still passing this test, since it never exercises concurrency. This is a genuine gap, not acceptable per this codebase's own convention: tests/schedule/end-to-end.test.ts DOES race-test this exact idiom via Promise.all for takeLease/reclaimLease. The enqueue spec text explicitly draws that analogy, inviting the same bar, but no Promise.all race test exists for enqueue anywhere (it has no caller in src/ and is only exercised sequentially here).

note: 5x (1500ms) is far looser than the fix's own reasoning needs: a real run above measured only ~12ms of spawn/kill overhead over the 300ms configured timeout (312ms actual). A mutation that silently doubles or triples the configured value (600ms/900ms) — explicitly named as a case worth guarding against — sails under the 1500ms ceiling undetected. Only a mutation that swaps in a much larger hardcoded constant (>=1500ms, e.g. 2000ms) or the real 60000ms default is actually caught (the latter via vitest's 10s test timeout, not the assertion). Tighten the bound close to the observed overhead (e.g. timeoutMs + a few hundred ms, or 2x) to catch multiplicative mutations too.

note: snapshotOf (tests/dispatch/end-to-end.test.ts lines 43-53) only branches on entry.isFile() and entry.isDirectory(); a Dirent for a symlink returns false for both (it is classified via isSymbolicLink() instead), so a symlink added or removed directly under the queue directory is invisible to the snapshot. Verified empirically: adding a dangling symlink, or a symlink to an existing empty directory, as a new top-level entry in the snapshotted dir produces a byte-identical before/after snapshot (same directories array, same files map) even though a new sibling filesystem entry now exists in the queue directory. This directly overstates the THEN's 'no sibling task directory added or removed' -- a sibling entry can be added via a symlink and the proof would not catch it. (A symlink to a non-empty directory happens to be caught only incidentally, because recursive readdir follows it and surfaces its target's files under the new path -- but that is not true for a symlink to an empty directory or a dangling symlink.)
